title: Knowledge check: Understanding Errors and Warnings

questions.prompt: For “Understanding Errors and Warnings”, which approach best supports a reliable result?
options: Inspect assumptions, run a small example, and verify an edge case.
Trust the first output without inspecting its inputs.
Hide warnings and skip validation to make the result look clean.
Change several unrelated parts at once so the cause of any result is unclear.
questions.answer_key: Inspect assumptions, run a small example, and verify an edge case.
questions.explanation: A reliable workflow turns assumptions into checks and uses errors, tests and logs as evidence instead of hiding failures. Reliable work makes assumptions visible and checks behavior before scaling up.

questions.prompt: Which item is explicitly listed under “Understanding Errors and Warnings” in the source curriculum?
options: Change unrelated settings before checking the input
Assume one example proves every edge case
Skip validation when the output looks plausible
questions.explanation: The source PDF lists “Syntax Errors” as part of lesson 196. The lesson retains the original topic wording.

questions.prompt: When applying “Understanding Errors and Warnings” to real work, what should you do before relying on the result?
options: Validate inputs and output shape, test a boundary case, and state limitations.
Assume missing and malformed inputs never occur.
Use the same method regardless of data type or the research question.
Remove inconvenient observations without recording the decision.
questions.answer_key: Validate inputs and output shape, test a boundary case, and state limitations.
questions.explanation: Write one positive test and one failure/edge test, then state what evidence would prove the check ran. Record assumptions and known limitations instead of presenting a demonstration as proof.
